Keywords: reset undo soft mixed hard HEAD commit staged unstaged restore
Description: Move HEAD (and optionally the index and working tree) to a previous commit. Modes per official docs: --soft (leaves index and working tree unchanged); --mixed (default — leaves working tree unchanged, resets index to new HEAD); --hard (rewrites both working tree and index to match commit — may overwrite untracked files, removes tracked files not in commit).
When to Use: Undoing commits, unstaging files, or reverting the working tree to a known state
Command Example:
# Undo last commit but KEEP changes staged (soft)
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# Undo last commit and UNSTAGE changes, keep working tree (mixed — default)
git reset HEAD~1

# Undo last commit and DISCARD all changes (hard — DANGEROUS)
git reset --hard HEAD~1

# Unstage a file (modern preferred alternative: git restore --staged)
git restore --staged forgotten_file.py
# Legacy equivalent:
git reset HEAD -- forgotten_file.py
Gotchas: git reset --hard overwrites working tree files and MAY overwrite untracked files. Working tree changes lost this way are GONE — commits can be recovered via reflog for ~90 days but uncommitted changes cannot. Always stash before a hard reset.

Keywords: revert undo commit safe public shared branch new commit
Description: Create a new commit that inverts the changes of a specific commit. Safe for shared branches because it adds a commit rather than rewriting history.
When to Use: Undoing a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch — the safe alternative to reset
Command Example:
# Revert the last commit
git revert HEAD

# Revert a specific commit (creates a new undo commit)
git revert a1b2c3d

# Revert without opening editor
git revert --no-edit HEAD~2

# Revert a merge commit (specify parent to revert to)
git revert -m 1 HEAD
Gotchas: Reverting a merge commit requires -m to specify which parent is the 'mainline'. Reverting a revert creates a double-revert — use cautiously.

Keywords: stash push pop apply drop list branch recover named stash create store export import
Description: Stash stores uncommitted changes in a stack of stash entries. Modern syntax: git stash push (git stash save is deprecated). git stash branch creates and checks out a new branch starting from the stash's base commit then applies the stash — very useful when git stash apply would conflict.
When to Use: Managing multiple in-progress work items without committing placeholder code
Command Example:
# Named stash (modern syntax)
git stash push -m 'WIP: CORS implementation'

# List all stashes
git stash list

# Apply specific stash (keep it in list)
git stash apply stash@{2}

# Pop (apply and remove — fails gracefully on conflict: stash NOT dropped)
git stash pop

# Create a branch from a stash (applies stash then drops it automatically)
git stash branch feature/recovered stash@{0}

# Drop a stash
git stash drop stash@{1}
Gotchas: git stash save is deprecated — use git stash push. git stash pop applies AND removes the stash. If apply causes a conflict the stash is NOT dropped automatically — you must resolve conflicts then run git stash drop manually. Stashes are local — not pushed to remote. git stash branch can also transfer stashes between worktrees.

Keywords: reflog recover deleted branch lost commit SHA git log -g
Description: When a branch is deleted its commits are still reachable via reflog for ~90 days (configurable). git reflog show is an alias for git log -g --abbrev-commit --pretty=oneline. Find the SHA and create a new branch pointing to it.
When to Use: After accidentally deleting a branch that contained unmerged work
Command Example:
# View reflog (show is the default subcommand, alias for git log -g)
git reflog

# Search reflog for branch name
git reflog show --all | grep 'feature/deleted-branch'

# Recreate the branch at the recovered SHA
git switch -c feature/recovered a1b2c3d

# Or use HEAD@{N} notation
git switch -c feature/recovered HEAD@{7}
Gotchas: The reflog is LOCAL — if the branch was only on a remote and you removed the remote tracking ref use git fetch to restore it. Reflog entries expire: reachable commits ~90 days, unreachable ~30 days (configured by gc.reflogExpire and gc.reflogExpireUnreachable).

Keywords: recover lost stash drop hard reset undo uncommitted discard fsck
Description: If you ran git reset --hard or git stash drop changes may still be recoverable through git's object database (dangling objects) via git fsck.
When to Use: Emergency recovery when git reset --hard or git stash drop lost important uncommitted work
Command Example:
# Find dangling blobs (recent uncommitted files)
git fsck --lost-found

# List dangling commits
git fsck --no-reflogs | grep 'dangling commit'

# Recover dangling commit
git show a1b2c3d

# Check .git/lost-found/other/ for lost blob objects
ls .git/lost-found/other/
Gotchas: git fsck recovery is not guaranteed — object garbage collection (git gc) permanently removes unreferenced objects. If gc ran after the loss recovery is impossible. Use git stash before any destructive operation.

Keywords: clean untracked remove delete build artifacts temporary files
Description: Remove untracked files and directories from the working tree. Use -n for dry run first. Use -f to force. Use -d to include untracked directories.
When to Use: Cleaning build artifacts, removing untracked generated files, or getting to a pristine state
Command Example:
# Dry run — see what would be deleted
git clean -n

# Remove untracked files
git clean -f

# Remove untracked files AND directories
git clean -fd

# Remove ignored files too (build artifacts)
git clean -fdx

# Interactive mode
git clean -i
Gotchas: git clean -fdx is VERY destructive — it removes .gitignored files including .env virtual environments and build output. Run -n first EVERY time. Irreversible.

Keywords: bisect binary search good bad regression bug commit run script exit code
Description: Perform a binary search through commit history to find which commit introduced a bug. Mark commits as 'good' (old) or 'bad' (new). Script mode: exit 0 = good; exit 1-127 (except 125) = bad; exit 125 = skip this commit (cannot be tested). Exit codes 126 and 127 are POSIX shell errors and abort bisect.
When to Use: When a bug exists now but didn't before — you know the last good commit (e.g. a tag) and need to find the culprit
Command Example:
# Start bisect
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v1.0.0

# Test current checkout, then mark it
git bisect good   # or: git bisect bad

# After Git finds the bad commit
git bisect reset    # returns to original HEAD

# Automate with a test script (exit 0=good, 1-127=bad, 125=skip)
git bisect run python -m pytest tests/test_auth.py -q
Gotchas: git bisect leaves you on a detached HEAD — always run git bisect reset after. Exit code 125 skips the current commit. Exit codes 126/127 are treated as normal test errors. Requires a clean working tree to start.

Keywords: worktree multiple checkout parallel branch simultaneously work repair move prune lock
Description: git worktree allows checking out multiple branches simultaneously in separate directories. Each worktree shares the same .git database. Key subcommands per docs: add, list, lock, move, prune, remove, repair. The main worktree cannot be removed. remove requires --force for unclean worktrees or those with submodules.
When to Use: Working on a hotfix urgently while mid-feature, or running tests on main while developing on feature
Command Example:
# Add a second worktree for a hotfix (from official docs example)
git worktree add -b emergency-fix ../temp master
cd ../temp
# ... hack hack hack ...
git commit -a -m 'emergency fix for boss'
cd -
git worktree remove ../temp

# List all worktrees
git worktree list

# Lock a portable worktree to prevent pruning
git worktree lock --reason 'USB drive' ../my-worktree

# Repair after moving main worktree manually
git worktree repair

# Prune stale worktree references
git worktree prune
Gotchas: Each worktree checkout is exclusive — you cannot check out the same branch in two worktrees simultaneously. Multiple checkout is still experimental for submodules per official docs. git worktree remove only works on clean worktrees — use --force for unclean ones. Use worktree.useRelativePaths=true for portable setups (requires Git extension; incompatible with older Git).
